newsitem.title: CHINA: China sets new curbs on stock trade by state firms.
newsitem.headline: China sets new curbs on stock trade by state firms.

text.p: China has imposed new curbs on the trading of shares by state-owned companies, barring them from making "speculative" deals, the official Xinhua news agency said on Wednesday.
The new rules did not ban all trading by state owned companies but they appeared to be part of campaign by market regulators to cool the nation's overheated stock markets.

The rules, issued by the Securities Commission of the State council (cabinet), the central bank and the State Economic and Trade Commission, barred state companies from using borrowings from state banks or providing funds to other entities to speculate in the stock market.
State companies that hold shares in listed companies for long-term investment purposes must also file a report with securities exchanges.
The rules also barred listed companies from using funds raised from public offerings to trade in securities.
Listed companies were also specifically barred from borrowing from state banks in order to trade stock.
Xinhua said state companies could open only one trading account for domestic share dealings and had to use their own name on the account.

The agency said some state companies had recently been using funds set aside for corporate development to trade in the stock market. Other listed companies had used capital raised from their own public offerings to speculate in the stock market.
It did not name any companies.
"This excessive speculation and improper activity is relatively serious," Xinhua said, adding that putting a stop to such practices was crucial for social stability.
China has announced a series of measures aimed at cooling its domestic stock markets which have surged more than 50 percent this year.
It raised the stamp transaction tax and announced the names of a number of companies found to have conducted trading irregularities.
Brokers say that Zhou Daojiong, chairman of the nation's chief securities watchdog, the China Securities Regulatory Commission, will soon step down. This has not yet been officially confirmed.
Xinhua said government departments would inspect state-owned companies to ensure they complied with the regulations while securities authorities would review activities of listed companies.
Future violators could be fined and their profits from such trading confiscated.
Misused bank loans would be recalled and no new loans would be extended, the agency said.
Responsible officials of the state-owned companies could be removed from office while those directing listed companies could be barred from any stock-related activities, it said.
